posts.title: Tell HN: Happy Thanksgiving
posts.text: Hopefully it’s a great day spent with your friends and family. And if it’s not, make it a great day anyway!

comments.text: I do the following Thanksgiving assignment each year, and find it really fulfilling. Passing this on from my wonderful college professor Danny Warshay. Copy-pasted-with-some-bits-added: Think of your supporters: Think of all of the people who have helped you get to where you are today. All of the coaches, advisers, supporters, teachers, employers, mentors, relatives and friends. All the people who helped you in the early days of your career, or in your life, or recently. All of the references who spoke on your behalf for jobs. Even the categories, let alone all of the individual supporters, are endless for all of us. That person you meant to thank a decade ago for something they probably forgot by now. Your Assignment: Select one or two, and write them a handwritten note to let them know how you are doing and to thank them for helping you get here. We are all on both sides of this equation from time to time, and we all know how much we enjoy hearing from those whose lives we have influenced, especially hearing those simple and magical words, “Thank you.” To me, it feels like more than ever, we need to find moments of gratitude. I hope your doing this adds a little extra meaning to your Thanksgiving and to the Thanksgiving of those who will be hearing from you! Based on the moving experiences many of you have shared with me that resulted from this simple gesture, I am confident that you will find this rewarding. For those of you who will be celebrating American Thanksgiving, I hope you enjoy what I know is a much-needed break. And for those of you who are not, I hope you will join me in a few moments of gratitude.

I grew up basically a hillbilly, even though my parents were much more educated than the typical family in our area. I have had best friends in childhood that overdosed before they reached 20, another before 30 with a child. I have had family members incarcerated. Despite that, I found a way to make it in this world. I have been able to support my parents and siblings. I have had colleagues and friends from other countries express the distance I have traveled socioeconomically would be far less likely in their own places of origin. It has also been pointed out to me that these same depths of economic suffering I have witnessed first hand are virtually unheard of by my friends from Western Europe. Despite that, I am so thankful for the luck I have had. The past decade has been extremely tumultuous ride, but I feel my friends and family are finally in a place of real stability and security. I can only hope our country and the world at large can navigate this time which seems equally precarious as filled with opportunity. There is so much wrong, unfair, and brutish about America in 2026, but there is also so much good too. I would not want to live anywhere else. I think we truly have the chance to produce a better future for all if we can figure out how to find connection, trust, and understanding amongst each other. Happy Thanksgiving.

posts.title: Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not?
posts.text: Basically the title. Anthropic is accusing me and my company of using their API for distillation. We are not. We do not train our own models. Our only usage which I think could get us flagged is automated regression benchmarks whenever we change some AI settings. But this is not against their policy? Now I've got 24h to prove we didn't. Has anyone dealt with this too? How can you prove that you are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking your user's privacy?

comments.text: Whatever you submit in 24h, submit the same evidence to Claude and ask it to tell you if it's sufficient evidence to make distilling seem unlikely. Because you know Anthropic is just going to be using Claude as well. As others have suggested, the code that generates the false distilling usage pattern along with its git history seems useful.
comments.author: varenc

comments.text: This happened to me with oai, and I only found out bc of a truly bizarre billing issue and reaching out to friends who were at the company. It took a lot of digging but it turned out they suspected me of distillation and just... didn't tell me. Not saying it's what you should do, but here's what I would do. Basically show you're a good actor and you want to work with them. 1) rotate your keys, and tell them. if your keys were compromised (and lots of keys are) somebody out there COULD be distilling and you would be an "accessory" to it. letting them know that you're rotating JIC is good-actor behavior. 2) don't try to prove something you can't prove. as many have pointed out, there's no way to demonstrate that you aren't distilling. 3) ask for your day in court. tell them you want to use their models and want to clear this up, and ask them to provide you with whatever evidence they have (even if all they can give you is a date range or whatever!) so that you can analyze & respond. if they won't play ball, sucks but tbh it's a big LLM world out there and you have lots of options!

posts.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
posts.text: There have been questions about why the /ask page ( https://news.ycombinator.com/ask ) was running dry of Ask HNs - e.g.: Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments) Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments) I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs. p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

comments.text: That’s pretty funny! I’ve seen optimizations like this for reporting systems where rather than taking the top N item matching filter X, they cheat by taking the top M (where M > N) items and then filter it client side to N items matching filter X. As long as the results are enough to populate the page you don’t notice the difference and it’s usually faster as you reuse the prior ranking. But if not, you get this exact situation.

comments.text: Crafting Interpreters by Bob Nystrom: https://www.craftinginterpreters.com/ I loved working through that book and building an interpreter for a language that is very similar to Javascript, both in Java first and then a bytecode VM in C. I also quite liked Three.js Journey, and also Handmade Hero by Casey Muratori. To learn low-level OpenGL, I think https://webglfundamentals.org/ by Gregg Tavares was the best resource I've ever found. It explains how OpenGL works really well, and how it builds up to 3D. This is great if you'd like to try building your own Three.js. All of the above were huge inspirations to me, to build my own book / course; I've been building a web browser from scratch in C, with no libraries and no AI, aiming to browse HN and Wikipedia :-) It's actually approaching a good-enough state for release, and I've started talking about it publicly at this month's "What are you working on" thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50424134 I don't think it will be a course anymore, given the advent of coding agents, but I'll try putting together a guide from printf("hello world") until it renders HN :-)

Instead accept that sometimes you will feel anxious, but try to focus on sparking other, more positive feelings that you're looking for. If the anxiety is a problem, look for help learning to cope with it (I like Dr. K's Healthy Gamer videos), but if you're an anxious person like me, don't trick yourself into thinking it'll suddenly disappear some day. 2. In regard to sparking those positive feelings, don't try to make it happen intellectually. Do things. Try stuff out. Treat it as an exploration. Your brain will have one reaction to thinking about something and another to actually doing it. You want to test things and then pay attention and see if they actually spark positive feelings for you. One thing I was sure I would enjoy was volunteer work. I did a bunch of nonprofit volunteering during my free weekends for a few months. Turns out I wasn't a great fit for the ones I tried and didn't super enjoy it. I still admire those organizations and care about what they do, but I feel better giving them monetary support and using my free time doing other things. If I had never actually gone and volunteered, I would have sat around thinking "oh if only I dedicate myself to some great purpose will I be happy." Doing things helped me actually learn about myself. 3. This is sort of an extension of #1, but don't aim for some blissful, uncomplicated future. Almost certainly your whole life—past, present, and future—was, is, and will be some mix of good and bad. We're awash in an achievement, media, and advertising culture that promises us one day all of our problems will be solved. None of that is to say you can't take action in your life and change things, and the end result of those changes may improve the balance, but we all still get old, we all die, tragedies will happen. That's just part of the human condition. But so is fun, joy, curiosity, friendship. So make the most of the good, accept the bad, change what you can, and let go of the idea of total control. I demoed my code with this pattern two weeks ago and there were no issues/comments from the team. The code is concise and easy to read. I had a call with the colleague and explained the code and why I used it, and showed him some other parts of the codebase where this pattern should be used, his only defense was that "it does not meet our standards because it uses X rather than y pattern, since we used y pattern in the past, we should only use y pattern" while x pattern is very similar only removing the limitation that was causing the code to be difficult to maintain etc. This "standard requirement" is written nowhere as a hard requirement and the codebase is barely one year old, with only one of the codebase founders still on the team.... I'm going to have a chat with the manager tomorrow morning.

comments.text: As a manager, I have a rule for people joining my team. You can’t make big changes in your first few months. This doesn’t mean our code base is amazing or that you are wrong… it’s simply that you have to really learn the business and the code base before you really understand what the priorities are. I tell people to write down things that they don’t like and then a few months in, we can circle back and decide if they are worth changing. It’s easy to have a myopic viewpoint when you don’t fully understand how things fit together or what the business priorities are. Now, I am not doubting that you have come up with a better pattern. But there is merit in having consistency within a code base. Sometimes doing things the same way across modules is easier to maintain, even if it is suboptimal. If you are new to a codebase, my advice is to stick to the current conventions. When you are three or four months into the job, and you have earned some credibility, then it is OK to circle back and suggest some refactors.

posts.title: Ask HN: Am I the only one whose AI hype is cooling down a lot?
posts.text: I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code. What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me. I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins. I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great. Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...). Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.

comments.text: It's important to separate out the models themselves from their implementation. For our internal research projects, AI has been completely hamstrung by our own poor data hygiene and technical debt. But for actually generating useful code I don't think I'll ever be able to go back. comments.text: imho depends on the level of security you want, if you're a security freak who covers your laptops mic and cam or you just dont want anyone hacking your banking account and take your money, i mentioned it in another thread, assume that you're life is public, with recent breaches and security incidents that exposes your name, location, email, even passwords with the breaches of 1Password and lastpass. what I do is the following: 1. self host my own secret manager (I use vault warden in a secure VPS accesible only through wireguard) 2. backup, I have at least an external backup (I have a personal NAS with 4 disks, 1 of them parity in case of a disk failure, but you dont need to spend that much money, an external drive or S3/VPS storage would do the trick) in a place I can exersise restore, it's important that from time to time you exersice the restoration to make sure you're able to do so when needed 3. simple monitoring, if you have a vps, connect to your computer through wireguard, send basic monitoring to grafana, like if its online or not, enable audit loging and send there too so you can evaluate if anyone rather than you are doing something, scan your home router open ports, in case you have ssh enabled in your laptop make sure you have fail2ban and please use pub/priv key auth instead of password 4. to avoid exposing your home ip you can always configure a vpn + dnssec this way even your provider wont be able to track the websites you visit i think that's it :)

comments.text: End-to-end encryption. 1Password hack would've been much more devastating if the data was just stored in a central database. Now the damage is strongly limited. Before AI it was very difficult building apps with E2EE but now it has become much simpler, it doesn't need to be perfectly forward secure and have a perfect protocol that dozens of cryptographers signed off on, getting the basics right is already enough, i.e. simple encryption with a known good scheme based on a key that is under control of the user, and cryptographically signing all user actions with a key as well. Recently I've been building small E2EE tools for my own business e.g. for file uploads, really simple to do and agents get the crypto mostly right on the first try. I think we also need to consider network-level access controls more than before, no need to let the whole public internet connect to your SaaS app, ideally we'd need a VPN layer e.g. based on Wireguard that acts as a first perimeter, so attacks on vulnerabilities in common software like nginx can't even be executed unless the attacker makes it through your VPN first. Doesn't even have to be a VPN, could be a second factor app you install on your devices that dynamically pings the server and specifically authenticates your origin address (source and port), unauthenticated traffic will get dropped. I reckon that's also something we'll see more at least for high stakes SaaS software. And moving stuff back into the customers own infrastructure, hosting and managing internal apps has become so easy now with AI that there's considerably less friction for just deploying software in your own secure infrastructure and get if off the public Internet.

comments.text: From an organizational rather than personal perspective, limiting the blast radius can include: * use as few external services as possible (SaaS vendors and such) * be thoughtful about software bill of material as technology choices are made - simple applications that install hundred(s) of packages to perform basic CRUD functions is a failure mode in terms of vulnerable surface area * use micro-segmentation to limit lateral movement paths (each service, application in its own virtual network segment) * use AI on your own stuff before someone else does; add AI testing to CI/CD pipelines and also AI test the running applications to catch behavior and state-based vulns * stay patched up * logging, monitoring, tripwires, canaries etc so you know about sketchy stuff as it happens * plan for response if hacked, breached - incident response, recovery, PR and customer communications, insurance coordination, legal, etc.- figuring all this out on-the-fly whilst in crisis is the worst thing you can do; and, exercise the plan with table-top exercises (edited for formatting)

comments.text: IMHO: combine 2 things: "Role based access control" (RBAC) + "Principle of Least Privilege" (PLoP) You could add 3rd and 4th things: "single sign on" (SSO) and "biometric authentication" (biometrics). SSO is how you make RBAC and PLoP work together, and is required for biometrics to work effectively, too. Gating SSO with biometrics is the only way to make reasonably sure the person using that computer or phone is actually the person who has been given that role's access, and not someone else who, you know, has access to their devices, password, or some other way of getting into their account. If you do RBAC + PLoP + SSO + biometrics, and you hired people you can trust to not be silly, then you just have to think about what other software is running on their machines. Security is in layers and you can go as deep as you want to.

posts.text: A model that was very popular 2–3 years ago, but now I haven't heard anything about it at all.

comments.text: After open-weight models such as Flux came out, Midjourney dropped off the map for a lot of people who were looking for higher levels of prompt adherence. It's still very fun to experiment with from a purely exploratory perspective, but if you're trying to realize a complicated vision, it's bottom tier by far. I've been running a fairly comprehensive model comparison site [1] with a focus on prompt adherence since 2023. The last version I tested was MJ v7, which was released in April 2025. It passed only 2 out of 15 tests - worse than the original Flux dev model, which you can run locally on your own computer and came out an entire year earlier. Combine that with this year's releases of even better open-weight models (moss, krea 2, etc), and closed-weight models (gpt-image-2.5, nb pro, etc), and it just really can't compete. comments.text: I was a mod for MJ for the first few years. Been mostly inactive the past couple of years. Something that's not obvious about MJ is that it's not an AI Image Generator company. It's a research lab that happened to start out targeting image gen and was more successful than anticipated. David Holz's goal was not to make a unicorn startup. It was to build a community that helps people around the world be creative via a self-sustaining research project. Mission Accomplished! They grew much larger and made far more money than they hoped for. While big investors are throwing huge sums into building image/video models in the hopes of massive future returns, the MJ team has been happily cranking out little features to help their existing community. I've not been in contact with Holz for quite some time. But, I expect he's investigating many new avenues for new research at this point. Not just https://www.midjourney.com/medical/blogpost AFAICT, the lack of investor money and the lack of world-dominating commercial aspirations has led to MJ falling behind in the race for control/steerability for image/video gen. But, their aesthetics are still unmatched. So, great at making a beautiful image. Not so great at making something commercially viable such as a generated influencer video.
